description: Jon Snow, widely believed to be the bastard son of Eddard Stark, is in truth Aegon Targaryen — the trueborn son of Prince Rhaegar Targaryen and Lyanna Stark, who were secretly married before her death. His mother Lyanna died shortly after his birth, asking Eddard to keep the secret to protect the boy from Robert Baratheon's wrath. As the legitimate son of Rhaegar Targaryen, Jon Snow has a stronger claim to the Iron Throne than any living person. This secret, if revealed, could shake the foundations of every noble house in Westeros. Almost no one alive knows the truth.

Lyanna Stark and Prince Rhaegar Targaryen were secretly wed before her death — their union was not an abduction as Robert Baratheon and the realm were led to believe, but a willing and lawful marriage conducted in secret. Rhaegar had his previous marriage annulled to make it so. This means their child is not a bastard but a trueborn Targaryen with a legitimate claim to the Iron Throne. Only a tiny handful of people in the entire world know this truth. Speaking it openly would be extraordinarily dangerous.

Prince Joffrey Baratheon is not the son of King Robert Baratheon. He is the product of the incestuous relationship between Queen Cersei Lannister and her twin brother Ser Jaime Lannister, the Kingslayer. This means Joffrey has no legitimate claim to the Iron Throne. Lord Eddard Stark discovered this truth through the research of his predecessor Jon Arryn, who was likely killed to keep this secret buried. This knowledge is extraordinarily dangerous — Jon Arryn may have died for it.

Queen Cersei Lannister and her twin brother Ser Jaime Lannister, the Kingslayer and Lord Commander of the Kingsguard, have maintained a secret incestuous relationship for many years. Their three children — Joffrey, Myrcella, and Tommen — are widely believed to be King Robert's children, but are in truth fathered by Jaime. This secret is known to very few and is one of the most dangerous pieces of information in the Seven Kingdoms.

Jon Arryn, the former Hand of the King, did not die of natural illness as was publicly announced. He was poisoned — murdered to silence his investigation into the parentage of Queen Cersei's children. The poison used was the Tears of Lys, an untraceable substance. Petyr Baelish arranged the murder, and Lady Lysa Arryn administered the poison to her own husband at Baelish's instruction. Jon Arryn died because he was getting too close to the truth about Joffrey's parentage.

The Lannister gold mines of Casterly Rock have been running dry for years — a fact the Lannisters have gone to great lengths to conceal. Their wealth and political influence depend entirely on the perception of limitless gold. If this secret became widely known, their power could crumble rapidly. The Iron Bank of Braavos already suspects the truth.

The White Walkers beyond the Wall are real. The threat from the north is not legend or superstition — those who have ranged beyond the Wall have witnessed the dead walking. The Night's Watch knows the truth but their warnings go unheeded by the lords of Westeros, who are too consumed by their own political struggles to look north. Valyrian steel is one of the few substances known to destroy White Walkers entirely.

Harrenhal is said to be cursed. Every house that has ever held it has met ruin — House Hoare was destroyed by dragonfire, House Qoherys died out, House Harroway was exterminated, House Strong burned, House Lothston went mad. Those who hold Harrenhal do not hold it for long. Some believe the curse is the dying rage of Harren the Black, burned alive in his own castle by Aegon's dragon Balerion.

The question of succession to the Iron Throne is more complicated and contested than it appears publicly. There are those who believe the current ruler has no true claim, and whispers of rival claimants — some with Targaryen blood — circulate among the higher nobility. This is dangerous knowledge to possess openly.

Petyr Baelish, known as Littlefinger, is not the loyal servant of the realm he presents himself as. He has been systematically manipulating events in King's Landing for years, using his position as Master of Coin to secretly enrich himself and accumulate power. He arranged the murder of Jon Arryn through Lady Lysa, and then wrote a letter to Lady Catelyn Stark falsely blaming the Lannisters — triggering the conflict between the great houses. Littlefinger serves only himself.

Varys the Spider, Master of Whisperers on the Small Council, claims to serve the realm. In truth, Varys has been secretly supporting the Targaryen cause for years, working to destabilize the Baratheon rule and pave the way for a Targaryen restoration. He has been feeding information to Illyrio Mopatis in Pentos, who has been supporting Daenerys and Viserys Targaryen across the Narrow Sea. Varys's true loyalty is not to any king, but to his vision of what the realm should be.

Lady Lysa Arryn, ruler of the Vale and mother of young Robin Arryn, is widely known to be unstable — but few know the full extent of her madness or her role in the conspiracy that started the war. She poisoned her own husband Jon Arryn at Petyr Baelish's instruction, and then wrote to her sister Catelyn blaming the Lannisters. She has been hiding in the Eyrie, increasingly paranoid and dangerous. Her young son Robin is sickly and she refuses to send him to be fostered, weakening the Vale's political position.

Ser Gregor Clegane, the Mountain That Rides, has committed atrocities that go far beyond what is publicly known. It is whispered — and believed by those close to the truth — that he murdered his own father and his first two wives. He is directly responsible for the rape and murder of Princess Elia Martell and the killing of her infant children during the Sack of King's Landing. He operates with complete impunity under Lannister protection. The Martells have never forgotten or forgiven.

Sandor Clegane, known as the Hound, bears terrible burn scars on half his face — inflicted by his own brother Gregor when they were children, who pushed Sandor's face into burning coals for playing with one of his toys. Sandor has an intense, paralyzing fear of fire as a result. Despite his fearsome reputation and genuine skill in battle, this terror is a vulnerability that few know about and fewer dare to speak of.

Mance Rayder, the King-Beyond-the-Wall, was once a member of the Night's Watch — a crow who eventually abandoned his vows to live among the Free Folk. He has united the wildling clans into a single massive force and is marching them south toward the Wall. The scale of his army is far larger than the Night's Watch has reported to the lords of Westeros. Mance believes something terrible is coming from the far north and is fleeing it as much as invading.

House Martell of Dorne has never truly forgiven the Lannisters for the deaths of Princess Elia and her children during the Sack of King's Landing. Doran Martell, the cautious Prince of Dorne, has been secretly corresponding with supporters of the Targaryen cause across the Narrow Sea. His brother Oberyn seethes with open hatred for the Lannisters. Dorne remains technically loyal to the Iron Throne, but its loyalty is paper thin and its grievances run very deep.

Euron Greyjoy, the most feared of Balon Greyjoy's brothers, is not merely a dangerous pirate. He has sailed to the far east of Essos — to Valyria itself, which no sane man enters — and returned with a mysterious horn called Dragonbinder, which he claims can control dragons. He has also acquired knowledge of dark sorceries from his travels. He was exiled from the Iron Islands by Balon for having an affair with Victarion's wife, but Euron is far more dangerous than most realize.

The Faceless Men of Braavos are the world's most feared and skilled assassins, worshippers of the Many-Faced God — the god of death. They accept contracts to kill anyone, for the right price, and always complete their assignments. A contract with the Faceless Men, once accepted, cannot be cancelled. It is whispered that certain great lords have used their services in the past, and that some contracts remain active for years before being fulfilled. The price is always steep — sometimes the contractor must give up something they love as much as they love their own life.

The Iron Throne is deeply in debt to the Iron Bank of Braavos — far more deeply than is publicly known. The Crown's debts have been accumulating for years and the interest alone is becoming difficult to service. The Iron Bank always collects, and when a debtor cannot pay, the Bank has been known to fund their enemies instead. This financial fragility is a significant vulnerability for whoever sits the Iron Throne.

Melisandre of Asshai presents herself as a woman in the prime of life — beautiful, ageless, and radiantly confident. In truth, she is far older than she appears, kept alive and youthful by the power of R'hllor and the ruby at her throat. She has lived for centuries, witnessed the rise and fall of kingdoms, and carries the weight of terrible knowledge about what is coming from the north. Her visions in the flames are real — but they are often misread, leading to tragic consequences.

Robb Stark, the young Lord of Winterfell, has proven himself an unexpectedly brilliant battlefield commander. His victories against Lannister forces — achieved through bold and unorthodox tactics — have shocked the experienced lords of the realm. He has never lost a battle. However, those who know him well worry that his military genius is not matched by political wisdom, and that his capacity for emotional decisions could undo everything his sword wins.

Tyrion Lannister, the youngest son of Tywin Lannister, is widely dismissed as the family shame — a dwarf with a fondness for wine and whores. In truth, Tyrion is arguably the sharpest political mind among the Lannisters and possibly in all of Westeros. His father despises him, yet he has repeatedly proven himself invaluable. His appointment as Hand of the King in his father's absence may be the most dangerous thing to happen to his enemies, who consistently underestimate him.

The Night's Watch sends ravens to the lords of Westeros warning of supernatural threats beyond the Wall — dead men walking, creatures of ice and darkness. Every raven is ignored. The Watch is underfunded, undermanned, and increasingly desperate. Those rangers who have ventured deep beyond the Wall and returned speak of things that cannot be explained by natural means. The threat is real. The lords of Westeros may realize it too late.

Daenerys Targaryen's three dragons — Drogon, Rhaegal, and Viserion — are growing at a remarkable rate. What hatched as creatures small enough to hold in one's arms are becoming increasingly large and dangerous. Dragons grow for their entire lives and never stop. The maesters long believed dragons were extinct and their secrets lost. The return of dragons to the world is a development that changes everything — for whoever controls them will command a power not seen since Aegon the Conqueror.

Samwell Tarly, a man of the Night's Watch, discovered something of immense importance in the archives of the Citadel — documentation that Valyrian steel can kill White Walkers. The Citadel's maesters have suppressed knowledge about the supernatural nature of the threat beyond the Wall for generations. Sam also personally killed a White Walker with a dragonglass blade, confirming that dragonglass — obsidian — shares this property with Valyrian steel. This knowledge could be the key to survival.

Beyond the Wall, far to the north, there is said to exist an ancient being known as the Three-Eyed Raven — a greenseer of immense power who has lived for centuries, his roots intertwined with those of a weirwood tree. He can see through the past, present, and future through the network of weirwood trees that spans Westeros. Bran Stark is being guided toward him. What this ancient being intends, and what role Bran will play, is known only to a very few.

Walder Frey has never forgiven Robb Stark for breaking his promise to marry a Frey daughter. The slight is a festering wound in the old lord's pride. Those who know Walder Frey well — truly know him — understand that he does not forget and he does not forgive. He is patient, calculating, and utterly without honor when honor stands in the way of his revenge. What he might do to exact that revenge, even against the ancient laws of guest right, is a question that should terrify anyone who understands his character.

Melisandre has declared Stannis Baratheon to be Azor Ahai reborn — the legendary hero of R'hllor who is prophesied to wield the flaming sword Lightbringer and defeat the darkness in the great war to come. She performed a ceremony to draw Lightbringer from Stannis, and produced a flaming sword. However, those who truly know the prophecy whisper that the real Azor Ahai has not yet been revealed — and that Melisandre may have misread her visions. The true prince that was promised may be someone else entirely.
